issues.legal_issue: A conviction for a capital offence cannot be sustained on a doubtful sole-witness account lacking corroboration when the surrounding circumstances do not establish the accused’s involvement.
material_facts: The prosecution case depended principally on one witness who said he saw the victim taken into a separate building, saw the accused leave without the victim, and then found the victim’s body inside.

The witness’s presence at the scene and reasons for being there were not independently corroborated; the doctor and the other person said to have been with him were not examined, and the victim’s movements before the incident were not established.
The building was across the road from the accused’s house and was apparently accessible to others, and the accused’s presence there was not fully established.
Although a blood-stained sickle was allegedly recovered from one accused, no blood-stained clothing was recovered from any accused, and bloodstains found elsewhere were disintegrated.
The case reached the Supreme Court as an appeal against an acquittal, and the accused had been tried for an offence carrying capital punishment.
issues.conclusion: The sole-witness evidence was not sufficiently reliable or corroborated, and the other circumstances did not establish the accused’s involvement beyond doubt. The accused were entitled to the benefit of doubt; the acquittal was affirmed and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under State of U.P. v. Satish (2005) 3 SCC 114, the last-seen theory is significant when the time between the accused and deceased being last seen together and the deceased being found dead is so short that another perpetrator becomes impossible. Under Joseph v. State of Kerala (2003) 1 SCC 465 and State of Haryana v. Inder Singh (2002) 9 SCC 537, sole-witness evidence requires caution and must inspire confidence and be beyond suspicion. As summarized in Ramnaresh v. State of Chhattisgarh (2012) 4 SCC 257, a conviction may rest on a sole eyewitness, but the account must be reliable, leave no doubt, and be corroborated by other evidence concerning the crime and the accused’s involvement. On an appeal against acquittal in a capital-offence case, the Court stated that interference was warranted only if the sole-witness testimony could be fully relied upon, with stricter scrutiny required. The prosecution charged the accused under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and capital_offense_case and case_depends_on_sole_witness and sole_witness_account_doubtful and (corroboration_lacking or surrounding_evidence_insufficient)

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.capital_offense_case: The accused are being tried for an offence carrying capital punishment.
predicates.case_depends_on_sole_witness: The prosecution case depends principally on the account of one eyewitness.
predicates.sole_witness_account_doubtful: The sole eyewitness’s presence, reasons for being at the scene, or account of the events is not sufficiently established to inspire confidence.
predicates.corroboration_lacking: Other witnesses or evidence do not corroborate material parts of the sole eyewitness’s account.
predicates.surrounding_evidence_insufficient: The physical and forensic circumstances do not independently establish the accused’s presence or involvement in the offence.

issues.definition: When an appeal against acquittal in a capital-offence case depends on a doubtful sole eyewitness and corroboration is lacking or the surrounding evidence is insufficient, the acquittal is upheld.
